I somewhat disagree. I think EA badly misjudged their audience. I also understand why gamers find pay to win objectionable. However, I think both non-pay to win and pay to win are legitimate approaches to games that can and will exist. To think about this for a minute set aside video games and let's think about racing.

Racing by and large depends on natural ability and use of that ability. In a 50 yard dash chances are good that the guy with the fastest twitch muscles and focus can beat those with less ability. But in a drag race for pinks, while driving skill plays a big part, there is nothing wrong with paying more money to have the faster car and beat someone with a slower car. Those two races are simply different animals. In the first it would be cheating to juice in order to increase your speed. In the second it is perfectly fine to spend your money on a faster car.

I think we will continue to see games follow both approaches and slowly separate themselves. On one side will be people who want a level playing field where the only contest is one of the player's skill ll. On the other will be people interested in and willing to pay more for the experience received from in game purchases. Game developers will need to decide which audience to focus on with which games.

It is always frustrating to not get what one wants. But game makers will respond to the market signals they get. Some of them will be mercenary and milk people from their money at every opportunity. Others won't. The market is big enough for both approaches. It will just suck to be otherwise interested in a game that is designed for the other audience.
